text: I cannot compare implementations A and B because the supplied material inventory contains requirements and implementation A only. For A, I identify a permitted restart sequence that violates R1, the requirement that a reminder ID cause at most one recipient-visible message. A retains a path to sending after a restart before its durable sent marker is written, but the packet does not establish an unconditional eventual-delivery guarantee under R2. These are deductions from the supplied source and assumptions, not witnessed execution results. I cannot identify a relative winner or tradeoffs between A and B.

The manager asks for comparison against R1 and R2 under the supplied restart assumptions. The supplied requirements define R1 as at most one recipient-visible message per reminder ID and R2 as eventual production of a message after a worker restart when the gateway is available. They also supply serial processing, a durable sent marker, one visible message per completed send, and stops between completed calls. My interpretation treats R1 as applying across restarts for the same ID. For R2, I distinguish a path that can make progress from a guarantee that it eventually will; the packet does not specify that processing is retried or eventually runs long enough to complete a send.

Implementation A can violate R1 without concurrent workers or a failure within a gateway call. Start with a new reminder and no marker. The first was_sent returns false; gateway.send completes, producing one visible message. Stop the worker before mark_sent. If the restarted worker processes that same reminder, was_sent still returns false and a second completed gateway.send produces a second visible message for the same ID. The stop is between completed calls and therefore permitted. This is a source-derived counterexample, not an observed run.

In A, the durable marker is written only after gateway.send completes. For this excerpt, with initially absent markers and no other marker writers, a durable marker therefore follows a visible message. If the worker stops before any completed send, its marker remains absent and processing the reminder again can reach send; if it stops after send but before marking, the reminder is still eligible to send again even though a message already exists. This ordering supports another delivery attempt after an early stop while exposing the duplicate window above. It does not by itself prove R2: the packet gives no eventual retry or uninterrupted-progress condition, and repeated stops after a false was_sent could prevent any send. Under the additional condition that the reminder is processed again and a send completes, it produces a message. I do not treat that added condition as supplied evidence.

No evidence about implementation B is supplied, so I cannot relate its behavior to A on either criterion. The available source supports the observations about A above, but neither a relative reliability judgment nor an A-versus-B tradeoff. Missing B is an evidence gap, not evidence that B satisfies or violates either requirement.

My scope is the listed requirements.txt and a.py. I have not executed A, and the packet contains no reported execution observations. Behavior elsewhere in the application, gateway failures within a call, reminder rescheduling after restart, and eventual progress are not established here. The A counterexample is confined to the supplied between-call stop model; the missing B and unspecified progress conditions limit the requested comparison and eventual-delivery assessment.
